title: Ramadan: the drummer
hookLine: a drummer walks the streets before dawn to wake people for suhur

cards: It's the dark hour before dawn in a Ramadan street, and the only sound is a small drum. A man walks under the balconies with a lantern and a stick, striking a little drum slung at his side.
He stops at a door and calls a name. Not a general shout: a name. The son of the baker.
The widow on the second floor. Upstairs, a light goes on. Then another.

teach.h: HE WAKES THE STREET FOR SUHUR.
teach.b: First, the job. The musaharati, as he's called in Egypt, wakes people for suhur, the meal eaten in the dark before the fast begins at dawn. Other places have other names for the same work.

teach.h: WAKE, SLEEPER, AND DECLARE GOD ONE.
teach.b: As he walks, he calls out lines inviting the sleeper to wake and to declare God one, and then he adds the names of the households. That's the heart of it: a whole street, known by name, woken one door at a time.
Third, a waking call in Medina.
Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tell that in the Prophet's own city, peace be upon him, Bilal used to call out while it was still night, so that sleepers would wake.

The Prophet told the people that Bilal's call did not mean the fast had begun: keep eating and drinking until Ibn Umm Maktum calls, for he calls at dawn. Two voices, one to wake, one to mark the start.
Fourth, the gentleness. Nobody wants to be shaken awake.

teach.h: A RHYTHM, A LANTERN, YOUR NAME.
teach.b: The musaharati comes with rhythm, a lantern and your own name, and he's gone before you're cross.
Alarms and phones often do the job now, yet in some neighborhoods the drummer still walks, and children still wait at the window for him.

Look back at this week: the farthest mosque in Jerusalem; mosques of mud and wood; mosques built today; your nearest mosque and its qibla; then Ramadan, with its lanterns, its cannon, and now its drummer.

how: In parts of Egypt and other Muslim-majority lands, a musaharati still walks the streets before dawn in Ramadan with a small drum, calling households by name to wake for suhur.

games.q: you're in Medina in Ramadan, eating before dawn. you hear Bilal's call ring out. what does the Prophet tell people to do?
o: stop eating at once; the fast has begun.
keep eating and drinking until Ibn Umm Maktum calls.
go back to sleep until the dawn prayer.
games.why: Bilal called while it was still night. the Prophet said to keep eating until Ibn Umm Maktum called, for he called at dawn.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll speak to first tomorrow, a child, a partner, a parent, a roommate, and how you usually reach them: a shout up the stairs, a text.

Now picture doing it the drummer's way: a soft knock, their name said kindly, a little patience while they come round. If you pray, hold that person in your prayer; if not, simply wish them a good morning before it comes.

wordCard.voice: Musaharati. The Ramadan drummer who walks the streets before dawn, calling each house by name to wake for suhur. Today's word.
